title: Heat Pump COP and Lift Explorer
description: Calculate the Carnot limit on heat pump COP from a stated outdoor temperature and supply temperature, to within 0.1, and use it to estimate the electricity and cost needed to deliver 100,000 Btu of heat.
creator: The Science of the Built Environment
author: Dan McCreary
subject: The Science of the Built Environment
chapter_title: Appendix A: Heat Pumps and Building Electrification

pedagogical.learningObjective: Calculate the Carnot limit on heat pump COP from a stated outdoor temperature and supply temperature, to within 0.1, and use it to estimate the electricity and cost needed to deliver 100,000 Btu of heat.
recommendedUsage: Read the outdoor and supply temperatures for challenge 1, convert both to kelvin, and type the Carnot limit. Press Check.
Work through the four challenges. The thermometer shows the lift between the two temperatures.
When the sliders unlock, change the outdoor and supply temperatures and watch the Carnot limit, the COP used, and the three costs update.
Switch the COP source to the seasonal COP of 2.5 to reproduce the Appendix A example, then raise the gas price until the heat pump becomes the cheaper system and compare with the break-even price.
activities: Predict the limit (10 min): For each challenge write the lift in kelvin before computing the limit.
Colder and hotter (10 min): Hold the supply at 100 F and lower the outdoor temperature from 60 F to -20 F. Then raise the supply to 130 F at 5 F outdoors. Record the limit each time.
Break-even (10 min): Find the gas price at which the heat pump and furnace cost the same, and check it against the readout.
assessment: Students compute the Carnot limit for 20 F outdoors and 110 F supply, showing both kelvin conversions.
Students explain why a COP above 1 does not violate conservation of energy.
